author: mdrewt
body:
## Slice uxd1 — Responsive viewport scaling (M-postgate-ux-design)

Fixes the three symptoms Drew's 2026-07-25 closed playtest reported from one root cause: the
canvas resized but the world did not, retina displays looked blurry, and small zones sat
stranded in the top-left corner.

**Pure-client render edge.** No server-module, schema, `game-core`, or wasm-bindgen change —
verified by `desync-guard` and `reducer-security-auditor`.

Items: r2-2026-07-26-010, r2-2026-07-26-011, r2-2026-07-26-012, r2-2026-07-26-013, r2-2026-07-26-014, r2-2026-07-26-047, r2-2026-07-26-048, r2-2026-07-26-049, r2-2026-07-26-050, r2-2026-07-26-051

### What changed

- **NEW `client/src/render/viewport.ts`** — a pure core (no DOM/Pixi/clock) owning the whole scale
  decision. `viewportScale(cssW, cssH, dpr)` picks an **integer** `deviceScale` (source→device, so
  one texel always covers a whole number of device pixels — that integer is what makes art crisp),
  aimed at `TARGET_VISIBLE_TILES` on the shorter axis and bounded by
  `[MIN_VISIBLE_TILES, MAX_VISIBLE_TILES]`, then derives the fractional
  `stageScale = deviceScale / dpr` and the effective viewport in SOURCE px.
  It exists as its own module because `world.ts`/`main.ts` are coverage-excluded imperative
  shells — math placed there is untested by construction.
- **DPR-correct backing store** — `app.init`/`renderer.resize` now carry
  `resolution = devicePixelRatio` + `autoDensity: true`. Pixi v8's defaults (`1`/`false`) were the
  retina-blur root cause.
- **Per-axis camera centering** (`camera.ts`) — `offsetFor` branches per axis: scroll-clamp when
  `mapPx >= view`, center at `-(view − mapPx)/2` when smaller. A wide-but-short map now scrolls
  horizontally while centering vertically, which the old single combined condition got wrong.
- **Fire-time dpr resize seam** (`resizeWiring.ts`) — reads `innerWidth`/`innerHeight`/
  `devicePixelRatio` at fire-time, so dragging between a retina and non-retina monitor re-crisps
  without a reload. `dpr` is a required third arg on purpose: an optional `dpr = 1` default would
  silently restore the blurry path.
- **`nearest` scaleMode** for generated placeholder textures — the stage is scaled by a device
  integer, so bilinear filtering would only blur crisp texel edges.

### Unit contract (the highest-risk detail)

Three spaces, never mixed: **SOURCE** px (`tile * TILE_PX`), **CSS** px (`window.innerWidth`),
**DEVICE** px (`CSS * dpr`). `FollowCamera.offsetFor`'s `viewW`/`viewH` are now the *effective
viewport in SOURCE px*, never CSS px. The mitigation is mechanical, not documentary:
`WorldRenderer`'s `#viewW`/`#viewH` fields are **deleted** in favor of one `#vs: ViewportScale`,
so the CSS value is not in scope at the call site. `stage.position` routes through the tested
`worldToScreen` rather than an inlined parallel copy.

### Review round

Six independent lenses ran against `git diff origin/master...HEAD`: `reviewer`, `red-team`,
`desync-guard`, `reducer-security-auditor`, `/simplify`, `tester`, then `verifier`.

Two findings were real and are **fixed in this PR**:

1. **CI-red blocker** (reviewer, reproduced by local `just ci`): ADR-0160's `**Decision:**` line was
   281 chars against ADR-0104's 240 limit, so `adr-digest --check` failed and `DIGEST.md` was stale.
   Shortened + regenerated.
2. **`init()` never applied `stageScale`** (red-team, with a fake-Pixi PoC): only `resize()` did.
   `#vs` was seeded to `viewportScale(1,1,1)` whose `stageScale` is `1` — identical to Pixi's own
   default — so any frame drawn before the first `resize()` used a transform computed for a 1×1
   viewport. Unreachable today only because `main.ts` calls `installResizeHandler` (which resizes
   synchronously) right after `await init(...)`; an `await` slipped between the two would have
   silently restored a broken first frame. `init()` now reads the window triple once, derives
   `#vs`, and applies the stage scale itself, so correctness no longer depends on caller ordering.

Also corrected: a `viewport.ts` comment claiming an operand-order overflow hazard that the
normalization bounds make impossible (max product is `1e6 * 8 = 8e6`), and two ADR statements that
had drifted from the code (the CSS normalization band, and D9's nearest-magnification identity,
which holds only at texture-generation time since the texture cache is not invalidated on resize).

**Adjudicated, not changed:** `/simplify` and `reviewer` both recommended deleting the unwired
`screenToWorld`. **Overruled on spec authority** — `M-postgate-ux-design.spec.md:34` assigns it to
this module by name, `:53` requires its round-trip tooth, `:55` explicitly scopes it as "ships for a
future milestone to consume, no listeners wired", and `:178` records it as a shared seam uxd2
consumes. Deleting it would put the code out of sync with the spec. The lens's *other* point is
accepted and carried as a follow-up flag: the "delete it later" note has no forcing function.

**Tester lens** was asked whether the `init()` fix needs a test and answered **no**, on the record:
mocking `pixi.js` would be a new one-off pattern this ADR already rejected, and a pure-module test
cannot observe whether the shell called `stage.scale.set` — it would have passed on the buggy code
too. Recorded in the ADR's "Known-weak verification" section rather than papered over.

### Verification

`just ci` **green locally** — exit 0, lint + typecheck + 1486 Rust tests + 74/74 evals + security +
wasm + client-typecheck + 1595 client tests.

The `verifier` independently re-ran the full gate and **proved four teeth bite** by mutating
production source and confirming the test fails:

| Mutation | Test that caught it |
|---|---|
| dropped the MAX-clamp floor `dLo` | `A3 BITES: MAX clamp binds` — `expected 1 to be 2` |
| `mapPx >= view` → `mapPx > view` | `C1b exactly fits → (0,0)` — `expected {x:-0,y:-0} to equal {x:+0,y:+0}` |
| dropped `/2` in the centering branch | `N3 leftGap === rightGap` — counterexample `[1,1,32,33]` |

author: parkjaehwan-906
body:
## 무엇을

`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` 의 정제 파이프라인(2차 검열) 수치를 **실배포 상태와 맞췄습니다.** 문서만 바뀌고 `.tf` 는 손대지 않았습니다.

## 왜

문서가 `batch_size = 10` / `BEDROCK_MAX_TOKENS = 2048` 로 남아 있었는데, 실제는 **7 / 4096** 입니다.

```
$ aws lambda get-function-configuration --function-name victoryfairy-dev-refine-bedrock
BEDROCK_BATCH_POST_SIZE : 7
BEDROCK_MAX_TOKENS      : 4096
BEDROCK_MODEL_ID        : anthropic.claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620-v1:0
BEDROCK_PROMPT_CACHE    : false

$ aws lambda list-event-source-mappings --function-name victoryfairy-dev-refine-bedrock
BatchSize : 7
```

Terraform 기본값(`environments/dev/variables.tf`)도 7 / 4096 이라 **코드와 실배포는 이미 일치**합니다 — 드리프트가 아니라 `10 → 7` 로 내리면서 문서를 안 고친 것입니다.

## 바뀐 것

**수치 정정**
- 다이어그램 `batch_size = 10` → `7`, "10건 묶어 1회 호출" → 7건
- 비용 "10 이면 하루 $4.5" → "7 이면 하루 $6.4" (`$44.8/N` 곡선)
- `BEDROCK_MAX_TOKENS = 2048` → `4096`. 이 값이 **AI 저장소 `config.py` 의 기본값 2048 을 Lambda 환경변수로 덮는다**는 점을 명시 (기존 서술은 앱 기본값이 곧 실효값인 것처럼 읽혔습니다)
- 미결정 항목의 "값은 5(게시글)" → `7`

**근거 교체**
배치 크기 산정 근거가 추정치("판정 1건 25토큰 → 2048 은 50~70단위, 게시글당 댓글 5개")였는데, `environments/dev/variables.tf` 주석에 남아 있는 **실측**으로 바꿨습니다:
- CloudWatch 폴백 통과 로그 7일 21건(하루 약 1,280 호출의 0.43%)
- 판정 단위당 약 24토큰 → 4096 의 수용량 약 170단위
- 게시글당 17~20단위 (추정의 3배 — 인기글이 `COLLECTOR_TOP_COMMENTS=20` 을 그대로 채움)
- `N × 21 ≤ 170` 이라는 **최악 케이스 보장** 기준에서 N=7 (이론상 8이 한계)

**추가**
프롬프트 캐싱 항목이 문서에 없어서 넣었습니다. 배선(`build_system_blocks()` 의 `cachePoint`)은 이미 있지만 현행 모델이 미지원이라 켜면 전 호출이 `AccessDeniedException` 으로 죽고, **서울 ON_DEMAND Anthropic 모델 두 개가 모두 미지원**이라 모델 교체로도 못 푼다는 점까지 근거를 남겼습니다 (캐싱 지원 모델은 전부 추론 프로파일 전용 → SCP `p-meobeew3` / 데이터 리전 제약). 2026-07-31 `list-foundation-models` · `list-inference-profiles` 로 재확인했고, `apne2.*` 프로파일은 존재하지 않습니다.

> 이 항목은 반복해서 되짚게 되는 내용이라 넣었습니다. 문서에 남길 성격이 아니라고 보시면 해당 블록만 빼겠습니다.

## 리뷰 포인트

- base 가 `dev_infra` 입니다 (dev_* 는 서로 disjoint 트리라 main 으로 열면 안 됩니다)
- 인프라 변경 없음 → `terraform plan` 무영향

author: callancapitolo17
body:
Closes #40. Ticket 08 of epic #32. **Decision: KEEP, not retire.**

## The premise was stale — Novig is alive

#40 was filed as "api.novig.us unresolvable — fix endpoint or retire". Verified on the wire 2026-07-30:

```
dig api.novig.us            -> 4 CloudFront IPs
POST /v1/graphql            -> 200 {"data":{"__typename":"query_root"}}
POST .../unauthenticated    -> 400 "must include two or more legs"  (origin reached)
price_sgps                  -> 112 rows in 17.6s
price_on_demand             -> fair=0.2144, route=partition, 4 cells, 8.05s
```

Production history agrees — from the research firehose, last 3 active days:

| book | sweeps with rows | median rows |
|---|---|---|
| fanduel | 100.0% | 112 |
| betmgm | 90.0% | 305 |
| **novig** | **69.8%** | **136** |
| prophetx | 72.6% | 894 |
| draftkings | 1.2% | — |
| caesars | 0.0% | — |

The DNS line in `bot.log` was a transient blip. Retiring this book would have deleted a working source.

## The real defect: 400 and 403 were indistinguishable

Novig's parlay endpoint has two non-200s that mean **opposite** things:

| status | meaning | frequency |
|---|---|---|
| `400 "Cannot price parlay"` | book declines **this combo** | common, normal |
| `403 <html>` | we are **rate-limited** | after bursts |

Both collapsed into a bare `BookTransportError:price` with `status_code=None` — so `sgp_fetch_health.error_class` could not tell "Novig won't build these combos" from "Novig has blocked us". This is exactly the diagnostic half #39 fixed for DK, never applied here.

**The rate limit is real and quantified:** 26 rapid price calls trip a 403; two back-to-back sweeps drove **100/100** calls to failure; the same combos recover after a cooldown. The ~7-minute sweep cadence has been hiding it. Epic #53's live-at-RFQ pricing is exactly the burst pattern that will trigger it.

## The trap this nearly shipped past

There are **two** `submit_parlay` implementations:

| function | serves |
|---|---|
| `NovigClient.submit_parlay` | on-demand (`price_selection_set`) |
| `scraper_novig_sgp.submit_parlay` | the sweep |

I fixed the client first, and the orchestrator's verdict still came back status-less. Caught by running the real sweep, not by reading. Both are fixed, and a test now pins that they are distinct implementations.

**Verified live against a real wire 403, both paths:**
```
sweep      error_class='BookTransportError:price:403'
on-demand  error_class='BookTransportError:price:403'
```

#39's `_accepts_on_decline` guard moves to `_shared.accepts_on_decline`, shared by both books (`draftkings._accepts_on_decline` kept as an alias). The guard is load-bearing: `submit_parlay` is re-imported per call so tests can monkeypatch it, and binding the kwarg unconditionally would `TypeError` on every combo in a pre-#40 stand-in — a silent zero-row cycle.

## ⚠️ Separate defect found, deliberately NOT fixed here

**The Novig *sweep* mislabels alt-line rows.** `_price_sgps` collapses every `TargetLine` of a game into ONE `fg_spread_line`/`fg_total_line` (`novig.py:232-247` — the loop overwrites, last target wins), resolves leg UUIDs once per **game** into `legs_cache`, then prices all ~33 of that game's targets with those **same legs** while stamping each row with its own `spread_line`/`total_line`.

Reproduced offline — 3 targets at totals 7.5/8.5/12.5 requested a single leg set (`H/A × O/U`) and produced 12 rows — and live, where totals 6.5/8.5/9.5 all priced `17.5439 / 4.1667 / 4.8544 / 1.4925`, hold 18.6%.

The `legs_cache` comment still says "two TargetLines on the same game (FG + F5)"; it was written when there was one FG target per game and silently degraded once the bot began enumerating alt lines.

**The on-demand path is unaffected** — `resolve_legs`/`_lookup_leg` do exact line-keyed lookup, and Novig's on-demand `0.2144` matched Caesars' `0.2167` on the same combo. Until this is fixed, `novig_direct` rows away from a game's main line are unreliable. Documented in `mlb_sgp/README.md`; **recommend a new ticket gating #42.**

## Tests

19 new (`test_novig_price_status.py`); 6 failed on the old code first. Covers 403-block, 400-decline, no-status-invention on connection errors, cross-cycle status leakage, success paths, both implementations, keyword-only binding, and the capability guard's degrade path.

**Suite:** 2182 passed / 7 failed — exactly the pre-existing worktree baseline (2163 + 19 new). DK/FD goldens remain red; they belong to #42 and were **not** regenerated.

## What I could not verify

- A live **sweep** end-to-end while rate-limited — tonight's games had started by then, so the sweep-path 403 was proved against the real endpoint via the legacy function directly rather than through `price_sgps`.
- Novig's on-demand latency measured **8.05s**, at the ceiling of #50's 8–10s budget (Caesars 2.84s). Left to #50 per your call.
- The live bots were **not** restarted.

author: michaeltaylor3d
body:
Closes DIG-Network/dig_ecosystem#1763.

## The defect

dig-node opens its HTTP surface ~30 s before the P2P content engine attaches. A read routed in that window skips Tier 2 outright and is answered by the public gateway — and said nothing about it. A fresh node, or any test that started promptly, measured the gateway and recorded the result as P2P. That makes it a correctness bug about **evidence**, not routing.

## The decision: (c) — serve, and expose readiness explicitly

Weighed against the alternatives:

- **(a) delay serving until attach** — trades availability for honesty. A node that refuses all reads for half a minute is a worse product than one that serves from the gateway, and it would break the existing "spawn → poll `/health` → read" harness contract (SPEC §7.8). Rejected.
- **(b) serve but mark the response** — keeps both, but a response-only signal still forces a caller to *issue a read* to discover readiness, and gives an acceptance test nothing to wait on except a guessed sleep.
- **(c) serve, mark the response, AND expose readiness out-of-band** — chosen. It is (b) plus the thing that actually removes `sleep 30` from the harness.

This is wire-visible, so it is stated normatively in `SPEC.md` rather than left implicit:

- **`X-Dig-Peer-Tier: attached | unattached`** on every served response. Captured **once at request entry**, before any tier runs, so it describes the routing decision that read faced — not whether the engine happened to attach while the read was in flight. Applied uniformly across whichever tier served the bytes. MUST NOT be derived from `X-Dig-Source`.
- **`GET /health` → `peer_tier: { attached }`** — the checkable wait condition. `status: "ok"` means live; it has never implied a usable peer tier, and now nothing has to infer that.

`X-Dig-Source` cannot carry this on its own: a gateway serve because no peer *held* the resource and a gateway serve because there was no peer tier *yet* are both `rpc`.

**On naming (#1738).** That ticket's complaint is that `X-Dig-Verified` reports enforcement while its name says verification. This header is deliberately narrow and named for exactly what it holds: whether the **engine was attached**. Not peer count, not reachability, not whether a fetch was attempted, and explicitly not verification. Both `SPEC.md` and the enum doc say so, so a second implementation cannot widen it by accident.

## Blast radius checked

gitnexus is disabled in the loop (worktree hangs), so this was done with ripgrep + a direct read of every call site.

- `PlaintextOutcome::Served` gained a field. Constructed in **3** places (all in `content_serve.rs`, all inside `serve_content_plaintext`'s own tiers) and destructured in **3** (two arms in `server.rs`, one core test). The compiler confirmed the radius: adding the field produced exactly **one** unmentioned-field error outside the files already being edited.
- `with_serve_metadata` — private to `content_serve.rs`, 3 call sites, all updated.
- `served_response` — private to `server.rs`, 2 call sites. Its five positional provenance args were collapsed into a `ServeProvenance` struct rather than growing to a sixth transposable positional (it already carried `#[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)]`, now removed).
- New `Node::peer_tier()` is additive; `p2p_content()` is untouched and stays `pub(crate)`.
- `EXPOSED_DIG_HEADERS` 10 → 11. **This is a cross-repo contract** (SPEC §4.3, mirrored in the superproject `SYSTEM.md` and consumed by dig-urn-resolver) — see "For the orchestrator" below.
- §5.3 endpoint ladder untouched: no change to endpoint resolution, no new hardcoded `rpc.dig.net`.

Risk: LOW. Additive on both surfaces, nothing removed, renamed, or re-meant.

## Tests — and why these fixtures

**`cold_start_gateway_serve_reports_the_peer_tier_as_unattached`** (dig-node-service, real HTTP). Not a mock of the window — `build_state` is the same constructor the daemon uses and does not attach the engine, so the reader node is genuinely inside it. Its Tier-3 fallback is a **second real dig-node** answering `dig.getContent` from its own cache, so the ciphertext, proof and chunk lengths come from the production serve path rather than being hand-built. It went RED on `<header absent>` *after* the `200` and `x-dig-source: rpc` assertions passed — which is what proves the fixture really is a cold-start gateway serve.

**`serve_reports_peer_tier_attachment_independently_of_the_serving_tier`** (dig-node-core). The nearest wrong implementation is `peer_tier = if source == Rpc { Unattached } else { Attached }` — indistinguishable from the real thing on any gateway-serve fixture. So this drives **one** capsule, locally seeded and chain-anchored, twice, varying only whether an engine is attached; both arms serve `Local`. Arm 1 is Local-and-Unattached (that impl says `Attached`) and arm 2 is Local-and-Attached, so it is satisfiable by neither the source-derived impl nor any constant.

**`health_reports_the_peer_tier_as_unattached_before_the_peer_network_starts`** — pins the out-of-band half.

Plus the existing real-provider peer-serve test now asserts `Attached`, so the two reads #1763 calls indistinguishable assert opposite values.

**Load-bearing proof** (committed first, reverted via file copy):
| revert | test |
|---|---|
| `peer_tier` capture → constant `Attached` | core two-arm test RED (`attach=false`); cold-start e2e RED |
| `/health` field → constant `true` | health test RED (and correctly unaffected by the revert above) |

## Evidence

Real cold start, real `dig-node run` binary, polling `/health`:

```
t=+0s   no answer
t=+5s   ok {'attached': False}
t=+10s  ok {'attached': False}
t=+15s  ok {'attached': True}      <- engine attaches
t=+20s  ok {'attached': True}
```

`status: ok` at +5 s with the peer tier down is exactly the window the ticket describes, now observable instead of inferred. The same live node confirms the header reaches the browser contract:

```
access-control-expose-headers: x-dig-verified,x-dig-root,...,x-dig-source,x-dig-peer-tier,...
```

Response-side: the two reads that were indistinguishable now assert opposite values — `rpc`/`unattached` on the real cold-start gateway serve, `peer`/`attached` on the real provider fetch.

## Gates

`cargo fmt --all` clean · `cargo clippy --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings` exit 0 · `cargo test --locked` full workspace **green** (463 + 246 + all integration suites).

## Version

`0.67.0 → 0.68.0` (workspace), `dig-node-core 0.24.0 → 0.25.0`. Minor: additive response header + additive `/health` field, nothing removed or changed.

## For the orchestrator (superproject, not touched here)

`SYSTEM.md` mirrors the exposed-`X-Dig-*` set as a cross-repo contract with dig-urn-resolver. It needs **`X-Dig-Peer-Tier`** added to that list. I did not edit the superproject.

## Deliberately left undone

- **Non-`Served` outcomes carry no peer-tier.** A cold-start read that 502s or 404s is still silent about the tier. `PlaintextOutcome`'s error variants have no such field and `error_response`/`not_found` are shared by unrelated paths, so that is real scope rather than a one-liner. Filed as a follow-up.
- **#1764 / #1765 are a different family** — chain-anchor enforcement policy, not tier readiness. Assessment in the ticket.

author: itsmylab
body:
Follow-up to #298. Three places still assumed one config directory, and each showed up as a session that ran fine but reported nothing.

## The bare footer

The status tray reads model, tokens and cost out of the transcript named by a hook event, behind a whitelist of directories we installed — and that whitelist was `$HOME/.claude` alone.

A session run under a second account writes its transcript inside *that* account's `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, so every one of them was refused as `"not a claude transcript"` and its footer came up bare: no model, no tokens, no cost. Exactly the sessions this feature exists to run.

The whitelist now spans every profile root, and stays a whitelist — the path arrives from a hook event and becomes a file read, so anywhere we did not install is still refused, extension check included. Tested both directions.

## Unsearchable sessions

The transcript scanner behind SpotSearch and the digest fallback walked the same single root, leaving a second login's sessions *invisible* rather than merely unlabelled. It walks every profile root now, for Claude and Codex alike.

## Plan rows collapsing

Rows were keyed on the CLI. Limits are per subscription, so two logins on one CLI are two rows — keyed on the agent alone they collapse into one, and "Claude Code" twice with different numbers is unreadable either way. Rows are now keyed by account and named by it, but only when the account isn't the default, so a machine with one login looks exactly as before.

## What this does *not* fix

The per-account plan chip needs a rebuilt hook helper. The installed `~/.canopy/bin/canopy-hook` on the reporting machine predates the profile-stamping change (its snapshots carry no `profile` field), so every status-line reading still lands in the default account's file. `tauri dev` / `tauri build` run `build:hook`, which recompiles it — a fresh build plus one session under the account is what makes its row appear.

Separately: notifications attributed to Terminal are dev-build behaviour by design, not a regression. `notify.rs` posts under `com.apple.Terminal` when `tauri::is_dev()`, because an unbundled dev build has no registered bundle id of its own; a packaged build uses `app.causeconnect.canopy`.

## Verification

- Rust 423/423 (1 new), frontend 1807/1807, `tsc -b` clean, eslint exit 0, `cargo fmt` clean, clippy shows nothing in the changed code.
- The transcript guard is the one fix with a direct test, because it is the one that silently ate data.
- StatsPanel has no test harness in this repo, so its row change is typechecked but not covered.

body:
## Outcome

Releases ACCELR8 Standard Mode v3 as a materially harder-to-game, research-auditable evaluation and adds the public release surface needed for research, operator, and social review.

## Benchmark credibility

- creates an explicit v3 benchmark/scoring boundary while preserving v2 replay
- adds public development fixtures and a fail-closed private official protocol
- closes hidden-state, state-fingerprint, and artifact/canary leakage paths
- makes scoring trajectory-aware and exposes every anti-gaming penalty
- makes advertised tools consequential and validates atomic failure behavior
- adds operational prompt-injection probes and passive, score-hacker, competent, community-first, and hidden-oracle controls
- reports deterministic 95% intervals, per-stratum results, paired deltas, collapse, robustness, tokens, cost, turns, refusals, infrastructure failures, and invalid calls
- upgrades the official manifest to schema v2 so turn/retry budgets are frozen with candidates and cases

## Public credibility surface

- adds a research-facing benchmark card and continuous credibility workflow
- adds an operator reality map grounded in current founder-residency/coliving operator descriptions
- adds contribution guidance, PR review gates, and structured validity/operator issue forms
- adds a static GitHub Pages showcase with explicit claim guards: scripted controls are not LLM results and public fixtures are not an official leaderboard
- adds a Pages workflow that reruns all credibility/release gates before deployment

## Verification

- `npm run typecheck` — passed
- `npm run test:credibility` — 16 files / 70 tests passed
- `npm test` — 37 files / 128 tests passed

### 💡 What
- Removed the unused `useSession` hook from `MenuItem.tsx` and wrapped the component in `React.memo()`.
- Refactored the heavy SVG map inside `Icons.tsx` into a module-level static dictionary called `iconCreators`, dynamically compiling only the active SVG, and wrapped `Icons` in `React.memo()`.

### 🎯 Why
- **`MenuItem` context subscription overhead:** Previously, every navigation menu item subscribed directly to NextAuth's `useSession()`. Whenever session updates occurred (e.g., focus change, periodic refreshes), all menu items were forced to re-render.
- **`Icons` element allocation cost:** The `Icons` component recreated an entire dictionary containing 9 large JSX SVG definitions on every render, causing garbage collection overhead and element allocation costs for every icon rendered.

### 📊 Impact
- Eliminates redundant context-driven re-renders of navigation items when the user session status refreshes.
- Avoids large redundant element allocations inside the render cycle of layout icons.
- Substantially reduces navigation/sidebar render overhead.

### 🔬 Measurement
- Run `pnpm lint` and `pnpm build` to verify clean compilation.
- Open React DevTools to verify that `MenuItem` and `Icons` components do not re-render unless their props change.

author: inexthome
body:
## Problem / root cause

You hit "The analysis response was not valid JSON" when requesting an AI red-team analysis. I checked Vercel logs first: `POST /api/floor/theses/.../analyze` returned `502`, and since that specific error message only fires when the Anthropic API call itself succeeded (200) but our own `JSON.parse()` on the response text failed, the request reached Claude fine — the model just didn't return clean JSON.

**I cannot reproduce this locally** — `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is blank in this environment (confirmed earlier this session; it only exists on Vercel). So this fix addresses the two most likely causes based on how the original code was built without ever being tested against a live key, rather than a confirmed root cause from a reproduction.

**Cause 1 — untested mechanism instead of proven one.** The original code relied on `output_config.format` (a JSON-schema constraint) to force clean JSON, and never defensively handled markdown-fenced or prose-wrapped output. This codebase already has a **proven, production-working** pattern for exactly this problem: `src/lib/moderation/ai-safety.ts`'s `parseSafetyJson()` uses a plain-language "return only JSON" instruction plus markdown-fence stripping before `JSON.parse` — for Anthropic responses specifically, not just OpenAI. I switched to match that exact pattern instead of the untested one.

**Cause 2 — thinking-token truncation.** Claude Opus 5 runs adaptive thinking **on by default**, and thinking tokens share the same `max_tokens` budget as the response text. The original request never set `thinking` at all, with `max_tokens: 2000`. If the model spent most of that budget reasoning through the critique (very plausible for a genuine multi-angle red-team analysis), the JSON output could get **truncated mid-string** — which throws exactly a JSON parse error, not a schema-validation error. Explicitly disabled thinking for this bounded, well-specified task (valid at the default "high" effort, confirmed no 400 risk) and raised `max_tokens` to 3000 for margin.

Both fixes are cheap, complementary, and don't conflict, so I applied both rather than guessing which one was the actual cause.

**Also added**: `console.error` logging of the raw (fence-stripped) model output when parsing fails, truncated to 1000 chars. If this somehow fails again, the actual content will be visible in Vercel logs instead of debugging blind a second time.

## Changed files

- `src/lib/floor-ai-analysis.ts` (+40/-18)

1 file changed.

## Security / permission boundaries

- No change in scope from the original feature — same admin-triggered-by-thesis-owner flow, same service-role write to `floor_thesis_analyses`, same "no rating/recommendation column exists" structural guarantee.
- The new server-side logging only happens on parse failure and only reaches server logs (Vercel), never the client — the user-facing error message is unchanged.

## Automated validation

- `npm run lint` — 0 errors (509 warnings, unchanged baseline).
- `npm run build` — succeeded.
- **Unit-tested the fence-stripping logic directly** (the one piece testable without a live API key) against four plausible shapes: clean JSON, ` ```json ` -fenced, plain ` ``` `-fenced, and JSON with stray leading/trailing whitespace — all four parse correctly after stripping.
- **What I still could not test**: the actual live Anthropic call with these fixes applied, since I have no working key in this environment. This is a best-effort fix based on the two most plausible causes, not a confirmed-and-reproduced fix — flagging that clearly rather than claiming more certainty than I have.
- No dependency changes, so `npm audit --omit=dev` is not applicable.

## Manual preview checklist (for you)

- [ ] **Priority**: click "Request AI red-team analysis" again on the preview and confirm it actually succeeds this time.
- [ ] If it still fails, the error will now be logged to Vercel with the actual raw model output — check `vercel logs` (or send it to me) and we'll know definitively rather than guessing a third time.
- [ ] If it succeeds, spot-check that the steelman/redteam/blind-spots read like a real, non-truncated analysis (not cut off mid-sentence).

## Rollback

Single-file, no schema, no data. Revert = drop this commit; the feature goes back to erroring the same way it did before.

author: mkpoli
body:
I checked every factual claim in the README against the code rather than against memory. Nine were wrong, stale, or missing. Based on #27 because it rewrites the same sections; merge that first.

**Wrong**

- **Test count said 115.** It is 151. The badge and the prose both said it.
- **"Source formats: JPEG · PNG · WebP"** in the comparison table. Ingest also accepts TIFF — `/\.(jpe?g|png|webp|tiff?)$/i` — so the table understated what it reads and overstated the gap to the servers beside it.
- **Cantaloupe's licence given as "custom (BSD-like)"**, where our own `docs/comparison.md` records NCSA, read from its `LICENSE.txt`. The README disagreed with the document it links to.
- **"`meta.json` is the only lookup on the hot path"** was never quite true — an image request always read a pyramid level too — and after #25 it is doubly wrong, since the metadata is usually not read at all. Replaced with what actually happens.

**Stale**

- **The `meta.json` shape in the R2 layout** omitted `rights` and `partOf`.
- **The timing table** was measured before metadata caching and conditional requests existed. The numbers are not re-measured here — I have no deployed instance to measure against — so they are now labelled as a floor rather than presented as current.
- **"a `profile` link header"**, when a `canonical` one is sent as well.

**Missing entirely.** Four things shipped and were never written down: conditional requests and entity tags, `Accept` negotiation on `info.json`, `rights` and `partOf`, and the metadata cache with its one-minute staleness consequence.

**Softened.** "This is the first IIIF Image API server for Cloudflare Workers" is now scoped to what I actually checked and when — the IIIF community list, awesome-iiif, and a GitHub search in July 2026 — and states the broader finding, that no such server runs on any V8-isolate edge platform. The claim is the same; it is now falsifiable and dated.

Numbers verified against a live run, not asserted: 151 tests, validator 33 of 33.

author: jfrench9
body:
## Why these files

Rather than chase a repo-wide percentage, this targets the code where thin coverage carries real risk: the **graph API** — the service that actually holds customer data — plus the two modules sitting at **0% while serving live traffic**.

206 tests, **no production changes**.

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `graph_api` | 70.4% | **75.1%** |
| Repo total | 76% | **77%** |

Per module:

| Module | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `graph_api/core/migration_service.py` | 15% | **85%** |
| `routers/graphs/memory.py` | **0%** | **92%** |
| `entity_sync/extract.py` | **0%** | **100%** |
| `entity_sync/{utils,configs,jobs}.py` | **0%** | **100%** |
| `graph_api/routers/databases/vector_search.py` | 48% | **70%** |
| `graph_api/client/client.py` | 50% | **60%** |
| `.../tables/materialize.py` | 29% | **42%** |
| `entity_sync/load.py` | **0%** | **52%** |
| `entity_sync/transform.py` | **0%** | 24% ¹ |

¹ macOS-capped by the skip guard below; runs fully on Linux/CI.

## What the tests pin, rather than just executing lines

- **`migration_service`** — the export/import mutual-exclusion guards, including 8-thread contention proving exactly one caller acquires. These are the only thing preventing two migrations from operating on the same customer database concurrently, and they had **no tests at all**. Also the rollback that restores `.pre-migration` files when an import fails partway (without it the customer's graph is simply gone) and the 0.1% node-count drift tolerance.
- **memory router** — all three gates (feature flag, shared-repo block, graph access) fire *before* any writer client is opened, and the client is closed on every path including the 404 and the raising ones.
- **materialize helpers** — the `DECIMAL`→`DOUBLE` cast, positional-NULL handling that keeps `COPY` column counts aligned, the `from`/`to` pass-through for relationship tables, and the path-traversal guard on the keyset snapshot path.
- **vector_search HNSW** — `_validate_identifier` against injection-shaped table and column names. It's the only thing between URL input and interpolated Cypher.
- **`entity_sync`** — shared-node dedup collapsing repeated `Element` rows while leaving `Fact` rows alone (deduping those would silently drop customer data), and nodes staging before relationships so FK constraints hold.

## One skip guard, and why it probes

Importing `networkit` claims pyarrow's `file` URI scheme (commit `a5b7baad`), which breaks pyarrow **filesystem** operations — in-memory ones are fine. The SEC knowledge tests load networkit and sort earlier in a full run, so the transform tests that reach `pq.write_table(..., path)` inherit a poisoned process. Since `pytest.ini` sets `-x`, that would halt the entire suite.

The fixture **probes whether local-file I/O works** rather than sniffing `sys.modules`. The collision is macOS-only, so Linux/CI still executes these tests and keeps full coverage of the path, while a local run degrades to a clean skip.

Verified the production job is unaffected: `entity_sync` does not pull networkit even with enrichment enabled, so the `a5b7baad` fix holds and this is purely a test-suite concern.

## One characterisation finding

`_classify_operation` only inspects the final path segment, so `/databases/{id}/memory/boost` is labelled `other` and memory work is under-reported in the operation metrics. Dashboards only — no correctness impact. Left as-is and documented in the test rather than changed silently.

## Verification

- Full suite: **11,884 passed, 24 skipped** (was 11,677 / 15)
- CI (Linux): **11,788 passed, 19 skipped**, `Run tests` 410s — none of the new tests skip there, confirming the probe keeps CI coverage intact
- `basedpyright`: 0 errors · `ruff check` + `ruff format`: clean
- Every new file also run in isolation, to confirm the guarded tests genuinely pass when the process is clean

## Not in this PR

Coverage on the SEC ETL, Dagster wiring, and CLI tooling is left where it is. Those are the pools that would move a repo-wide number most, and they're also where unit tests simulate infrastructure rather than verify it — which is the failure mode that produced the LocalStack/moto bug fixed in #980.

body:
Prototypes only — nothing under `app/prototypes/` ships, and no real surface changed. Branched off `main` so this carries only the client-record work, not the rest of `fix/session-time-integrity`.

## What's here

**`/prototypes/client-record-final`** — one record in three containers (panel, modal, page-width), plus the Notion-style expand: the modal becomes the full page in place, the way `SessionFullscreenOverlay` does, without touching the URL.

**`/prototypes/client-history`** — the history section alone, five ways, after it read as a bag of unrelated things three times running. The finding: the columns were never the problem, the **unit** was. A studio relationship is a sequence of nights; money and notes are properties of a night, not peers of it.

**`/prototypes/client-record-shotgun`** — seven whole records on one axis, phone and web side by side, with two audits above them:

- **Audit 1 — what the record says twice.** Six facts the current page states in two places. Variants 1–6 each kill more of them.
- **Audit 2 — why you opened it, and how far down the answer is.** The speed problem, and what variant 7 is built against.

## Variant 7

Standing notes ("the rider") leave the dated history and sit above the fold, because an engineer's notes are mostly recall instructions — the mic, the chain, who runs the desk — and those are true every time the client books. Burying them in history means reading the past to find out about the future. The composer picks which kind of note you're writing as you write it. Blocks with no answer today are absent, not empty.

## Also fixed

A month header that disagreed with its own rows: a deposit shown inside July wasn't counted in July's take.

`tsc --noEmit` clean, `npm run lint` clean (warnings only, all pre-existing). Verified in the browser at 1280 and 390.

body:
## Why

The circuit-aware queue worker is qualified as a standalone runtime, but applications should not have to assemble its queue provider, timeout layer, circuit coordinator, execution gate, shared adapter, processor, and facade manually.

## What changed

- add `DataLoomCircuitQueueWorker`
- add `DataLoomCircuitQueueWorkerSpec`
- add `DataLoomBuilder.circuitQueueWorkerConfiguration(...)`
- add `DataLoom.circuitQueueWorker`
- keep the direct and circuit-aware worker capabilities mutually exclusive
- make the most recent worker configuration method effective
- require an explicit durable circuit state store
- validate recovery/acquisition/transition scopes during build
- apply the existing queue-provider timeout before shared circuit adaptation
- preserve scheduler timeout as an independent boundary
- keep queue submission independently configurable
- add deterministic builder/facade tests
- add external JVM/iOS consumer coverage
- add API documentation and an audit checkpoint

## Safety decisions

- no implicit in-memory circuit store
- no inferred broad circuit scope
- no queue scope reused as scheduler circuit policy
- invalid provider or operation scopes fail during build before store/provider access
- build performs no clock read, identifier generation, queue operation, state-store access, timeout execution, scheduling, synchronization, or coroutine launch
- `DataLoom` retains a default-null getter for source compatibility with custom pre-V1 implementations
- enriched circuit-worker results are not collapsed into legacy `QueueWorkerRunResult`

## Focused evidence

The pull-request-only macOS lane produced clean implementation head `2cb34309d40004b295cc23cb92b19ea39034fd8b` and completed:

- runtime JVM tests
- `iosSimulatorArm64Test`
- external-consumer compilation for JVM, `iosArm64`, `iosSimulatorArm64`, and `iosX64`
- exact JVM and Kotlin/Native ABI generation
- runtime and Apple ABI checks
- public ABI-boundary validation
- Apple release XCFramework assembly
- facade, worker, circuit, and API-index documentation updates
- removal of temporary workflow and patch helpers

The final review commit records that evidence without changing runtime behavior.

## Final-head validation

All permanent checks passed on `4cd53cc17547896dc329926abb4886fbeb9236cc`:

- Pull Request Validation #335
- Android Validation #173, including the Room managed-device test
- Apple Platform Validation #183, including XCFramework slice verification, exported-header audit, and Swift smoke compilation

## Remaining DL-040 work

- separately configured circuit protection for queue-worker scheduling
- transport and storage timeout/circuit assembly
- protocol-specific connection/request/idle adapters
- production KMP iOS retry/circuit persistence
- manual retry/reclassification and circuit administration
- complete observability
- multi-process, process-death, restart, contention, and AC-FUNC-004 evidence

Tracks #94.

body:
<!-- Keep this PR as draft until it is ready for review. -->

HUMAN:

Ran the OpenHands server locally; this was also failing when installing from `npm` as well as on dev.

AGENT:

Verified the released automation package starts in the same isolated `uv` environment as Uvicorn. The process reached application startup and `GET /api/automation/health` returned HTTP 200 with `{"status":"ok"}`.

---

## Why

The local stack could fail to start the automation backend because `uvx --from` did not guarantee that the `uvicorn` executable and `openhands-automation` package shared an environment. Launching through `uv run --with ... python -m uvicorn` keeps both imports in one isolated environment.

## Summary

- Launch the automation backend through `uv run --no-project` for PyPI versions and git refs.
- Keep launcher documentation and focused command tests aligned with the runtime behavior.

## Issue Number

Fixes #16217

## How to Test

1. Run `npx vitest run __tests__/scripts/dev-with-automation.test.ts __tests__/bin/agent-canvas.test.ts` (48 tests pass).
2. Run `npm run lint` (passes; Node emits the existing `module.register()` deprecation warning).
3. Start the generated command with the required automation environment variables:
   `uv run --no-project --with openhands-automation==1.5.0 python -m uvicorn openhands.automation.app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 18991`
4. Request `http://127.0.0.1:18991/api/automation/health` and confirm the response is HTTP 200 with `{"status":"ok"}`. In local validation the service reported `Application startup complete` and became healthy after 31 seconds on a cold start.

## Video/Screenshots

Not applicable; this changes backend process launching with no visual UI change.

## Type

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor
- [ ] Breaking change
- [ ] Docs / chore

## Notes

The first launch may spend time resolving and downloading the isolated package environment before Uvicorn starts.

body:
## Breaking change

## Proposed change

Reroute the six broadcast-backed vehicle binary sensors — awake/connectivity,
user presence, and the four doors — to the vehicle's own unsolicited VCSEC
`VehicleStatus` broadcasts when it is BLE paired. Nothing changes for an
unpaired vehicle; it keeps its stream/polling sensors.

A new per-vehicle BLE data manager holds the direct Bluetooth client (the same
one the command router uses, read directly rather than through the router),
registers the persistent VCSEC listeners, and tracks a connection generation so
availability follows the live link. A paired sensor is strictly local: its value
is valid only in the generation it was received in, it goes unavailable on link
loss, and it never falls back to the stream or cloud. Unknown closure and
sleep/presence enums resolve to unavailable rather than a false state. No INFO
poll is issued; broadcasts are received only while a command already holds the
link open.

This is the first of a stacked series that moves the cheapest-source vehicle
values onto the local Bluetooth link. It builds on #176296 (its base branch),
which adds the BLE command routing this reuses.

author: shanehoffman
body:
## Summary
`design/tokens.css` shipped one state-change curve and no exit-specific duration, so every exit in the app ran at the same length as the entrance it undid. An exit plays after a decision the user has already made, so it should run shorter — this adds `--dur-exit` (130ms, ~2/3 of `--dur-settle`) and applies it to the two real exits in the app.

## Changes
- New `--dur-exit` (130ms) and its gated sibling `--dur-move-exit`, opening the Layer 3 duration scale.
- `.inbox__slot`'s collapse for a **filed row** now runs on `--dur-exit` (it has no entrance to pair with — `1fr` is its resting state).
- The filed toast's `transition` shorthand is split: the base rule keeps the arrival at `--dur-settle`, and `.inbox__toast--fading` states its own quicker exit. `TOAST_FADE_MS` follows to 130 so the JS unmount timer keeps mirroring the CSS.
- A separate exit **curve** was considered and refused, and the reasoning is recorded in `DESIGN_SYSTEM.md` §4: this app's exits are opacity fades plus one layout collapse, and an accelerating exit curve would hold the surface near full opacity before snapping it away — the same hesitation `--ease-standard` was already chosen to remove from hover.
- Two exits deliberately keep their own duration, each carved out in §4 so a later pass doesn't "finish the job": the placeholder's vanish-left already ran at 71% of its own entrance (`--dur-enter`, not `--dur-settle`) before this change, and the spirit-mark's aura fade-out is a settle-back on the app's one continuous motion, not a dismissal.
- New `designTokens.test.ts` assertion gating the pair rule itself (`--dur-exit < --dur-settle`), since every other check in that file gates which token a leg took, not the relative sizes.
- A code-review pass (already committed on this branch, `98fd6df`) caught a real nesting bug: the placeholder's row sits inside an `.inbox__slot`, the same class a filed row's slot uses, so retiming the outer slot silently truncated the placeholder's own 200ms vanish. Fixed with `.inbox__slot:has(.inbox__row--placeholder)`, and §4 gained the general rule: an exit nested inside another exit is timed by the outer one.

## Out of scope, and why
- **Menu / palette / dialog dismissal** — not applicable. `Select`, the command palette and every dialog unmount on close rather than transitioning out (a deliberate decision from #109, `f81f3db`); giving one a real exit would mean keeping a listbox mounted and transitioning `display` with `allow-discrete`, against the ARIA wiring and the "list is gone" test assertions.

## Test plan
- `pnpm exec eslint . --max-warnings=0`, `pnpm test` (317 tests), `pnpm build` all green.
- `pnpm tauri:build --no-bundle` (release, `--features parakeet`) compiles and links clean.
- Confirmed the new assertion is a real gate, not a tautology, by temporarily inverting `--dur-exit` to 250ms and observing the expected failure before reverting.

author: oddharsh
body:
## Claim card

Per [UNDERSTANDING-REVIEW.md](https://github.com/oddharsh/site/blob/main/UNDERSTANDING-REVIEW.md). Scale: UI/behavior, touching a build tripwire.

**Intended model.** Remove the whole View Transition layer: the cross-document opt-in, the CSS choreography it drove, and the same-document `startViewTransition` wrappers. The boundary is *all three or none*, and that is the non-obvious part of the change. Removing the CSS alone would leave the JS wrappers falling back to the UA's default root cross-fade, which is **slower** than what ships today. A reviewer who reads this as "delete some CSS" will mis-scope it.

**Prediction.** A visitor clicking any internal link gets the next page with no fade and no window zoom. Concretely: `pageswap` fires with `e.viewTransition === null`; no element has a computed `view-transition-name`; the CSSOM holds zero `::view-transition` rules. The Run palette, note popovers, and `/lens` tabs commit their state change on the click's own frame rather than one frame later. Nothing else about any page changes.

**Likely misconception / first plausible failure.** A white flash on navigation. The transition was pinning the desktop/taskbar/icons snapshot across the nav specifically to prevent one, and `writing.js` carried a comment recording that `/writing` white-flashed *without* the opt-in — which reads as a direct argument against this PR. The mechanism that makes it safe anyway: `html` itself paints the Bliss gradient (set in `chrome.js`, `index.html`, and `lwe-base.css`), so there is no white frame for the missing snapshot to expose. I had been reading that background as belt-and-braces; it is the thing standing in for the snapshot, and the comments now say so. The second misconception is the scoping one above.

**Evidence.**
- `pageswap` probe on a real cross-page navigation against the **built** output (not the dev tree — `/lens.html` only exists post-build): reports `"none"`, no ViewTransition attached.
- Computed-style sweep: 0 elements carrying a `view-transition-name`; 0 `::view-transition` rules in the CSSOM. An earlier run of this same probe returned the *old* rules and caught itself — that was a cached stylesheet, confirmed by a cache-busted `fetch` of `/luna.css` before re-running.
- `/writing` after navigation: `html` background is the Bliss gradient, and desktop + taskbar + icons are all present.
- Run palette across all four open/close paths (⌘K toggle, Esc on input, titlebar ×, native `cancel`), with the input focused synchronously. Note popovers open, cascade-position, stack two, Esc closes the topmost. `/lens`: five view modes, six lens tabs, `?lens=` sync intact, no console errors.
- Gates: 60 contract tests, 78 routes, 47 cal tests, `pages:check`, `build`, `perf-budget`.
- The new inverted tripwire proved itself before merge: it hard-failed the build on `horizon.html` until I scoped it to CSS only, which is exactly the "guard fires on its own documentation" case it now avoids.

**Remaining uncertainty.**
- **Engine coverage.** Verified in Chromium only. Safari also implements cross-document View Transitions and could differ on first-paint background timing; I did not check it. Firefox never implemented the opt-in, so it is unaffected by construction.
- **The flash is proven by mechanism, not by frames.** A transient one-frame flash is not something a scripted check can prove absent. I verified the causal path (`html` paints the gradient) and the post-navigation steady state, not a frame-by-frame capture.
- **Shell dictionaries go stale on merge.** `holding/a-dict` and `holding/p-dict` still encode the pre-change shell bytes. Per CLAUDE.md those roll from the *deployed* build after merge (`npm run shell:roll`), so early post-merge visitors get a worse dcz delta ratio until that runs. Compression efficiency only, not correctness.
- **The perf claim is an argument, not a field measurement.** Bytes and the prerender/animation overlap are measured; the actual LCP/INP effect on real visitors is not. RUM is the source that would settle it, and I did not wait for it.

---

## Why

Every internal page is prerendered on hover-intent (the speculation rules in `index.html`, eagerness `"moderate"`), so by click time the next document is already rendered and activation costs nothing. The cross-document transition then spent ~200ms of window minimize/restore choreography animating over a navigation that had nothing left to wait for.

Two features that each look like a win wanted opposite things. The prerender makes the page arrive sooner; the transition could only make it *appear* later. Firefox never implemented the opt-in and always cut instantly, which turned out to be the right call.

## What came out

Removed in full rather than shortened, because a faster wrong animation is still an animation nobody asked for.

- The `@view-transition { navigation: auto }` opt-in from all 22 declaration sites (`luna.css`, `index.html`'s inline block, `lwe-base.css`, the worker chrome in `chrome.js` + `writing.js`, cal's `templates.js`, 17 garage pages) and from `lwe-pipeline/generate.mjs`, which baked it into every generated LWE page.
- The whole choreography block in `luna.css`: the `axp-window` name, the frozen desktop/taskbar/icons groups, the plus-lighter white-blink fixes, the `axp-open`/`axp-close` directional pair. With the opt-in gone, every one of those rules matched nothing.
- The same-document `startViewTransition` wrappers in `nav.js` (Run palette), `notepad.js` (note popovers), and `lens.js` (view + lens tabs, vs toggle, counterfactuals). **Leaving these would have been a regression, not a no-op**: without the CSS to steer them they fall back to the UA's default root cross-fade, which is slower than what shipped.
- `nav.js`'s `pageswap`/`pagereveal` listeners, which ran on every navigation to tag a transition type for rules that no longer exist.

Unwrapping the callbacks also removes a trap the code kept working around. `startViewTransition` **defers** its callback, so `openNote()` had to put focus and measurement inside it (a popover is `display:none` until `showPopover`), `lens.js`'s `setVsChrome` had to flip its flag outside it because `syncUrl` read the flag synchronously, and `setLens` passed `animate:false` outright. Those calls now simply run in order.

## Guardrails

`build.mjs` check 3 is **inverted, not deleted**. It used to pin the three white-blink rules; it now fails the deploy if any source re-adds the at-rule. It scans CSS only (`<style>` bodies for HTML, comment-stripped source elsewhere) so `/garage/horizon` can quote the rule while explaining the removal, rather than the guard firing on its own documentation.

`/garage/vt-check` + `/garage/vt-b` keep their own opt-in and are exempt: that pair is a diagnostic mule wired to no shell, and it probes the platform, not us. Its stale "last shell navigation transitioned" breadcrumb (which read a `sessionStorage` key `nav.js` no longer writes) is replaced by a plain statement that the site doesn't opt in.

The `html` Bliss gradient is now **load-bearing** rather than belt-and-braces. It existed because the transition froze the root group; without a held snapshot covering the gap, `html`'s own background *is* the first paint. Comments at all three sites say so now.

## Docs corrected where they asserted this shipped

Both `/garage/horizon` cards lose their "✓ shipped on the site" tag. This is exactly the stale-card failure that page is most prone to, and one of them already claimed the cross-doc transition had been removed while the code still carried it. Also: a `/garage/teardown` quiz explanation that stated "the site does use view transitions between navigations", `CLAUDE.md`, and `design/README.md`.

`scripts/inp-lab.mjs` loses its VT-on vs reduced-motion A/B, which would now measure the same code twice. It keeps the per-interaction attribution that was the point of the harness.

## Measured

Brotli q11, what actually ships:

| file | delta |
|

author: isuttell
body: Fixes SPL-256. `ziw-code-review` resolved its review target from ambient session state (cwd, checked-out branch, `gh pr view` with no argument). During the review of PR #247 it forked a background agent that reviewed PR #226 — a different, already-merged diff — and returned a confident, well-formed report. The reviewer happened to notice. A wrong-diff review is indistinguishable from a passing review, and the orchestrator treats a verdict as the evidence that gates a merge, so a false green is worse than no verdict. ## Reproduction (run before the fix) The pre-fix resolution logic lived entirely in `SKILL.md` prose, not in executable code — there was no resolver to call. So the reproduction drives the prose-directed commands from a worktree unrelated to the named target, which is exactly what the forked agent did. Handed target: **PR #247** / `spl-234-flag-key-uniqueness` / head `1178288e0a61ddf837bb4b3c661d8c424b44e363`. Ambient worktree: `/private/tmp/spl-118-flag-editing` (a live session checkout for a different ticket). ``` $ git branch --show-current -> spl-118-flag-editing $ git rev-parse HEAD -> 6fc11883a03fe2779fde44577f0a7ec344cc7db2 $ gh pr view --json number,headRefOid -> {"number":245,"headRefOid":"4b8ddce33914532939cb8029a3b03a797e57a1ef", ...} ``` Ambient resolution selected **PR #245** at a head SHA that matches neither the named target nor even the local checkout. Same failure shape as the incident. Same worktree, after the fix: ``` $ node scripts/resolve-review-target.mjs ziw-code-review requires an explicit review target. Pass exactly one of --pr , --branch , or --range ... The working directory, the checked-out branch, and `gh pr view` without an argument are deliberately not consulted... exit=2 $ node scripts/resolve-review-target.mjs --pr 247 --repo zaks-io/splitch --json { "prNumber": 247, "headSha": "1178288e0a61ddf837bb4b3c661d8c424b44e363", ... } exit=0 ``` ## What changed - **`scripts/resolve-review-target.mjs`** (new) — the only sanctioned source of a review target. Takes exactly one of `--pr` / `--branch` / `--range`, resolves a pinned full head SHA from the code host or remote (never from the local checkout), and exits `2` naming the missing argument when no target was passed. Ambiguous or unrecognized arguments are also hard stops. `buildForkBriefing` emits the block a forked reviewer receives verbatim: repo, PR number, head SHA, diff range, plus an explicit prohibition on re-resolving from ambient state. - **`.agents/skills/ziw-code-review/SKILL.md`** — new `Review Target` section makes the resolver mandatory and deletes the ambient fallback; `Scope`, `Independent Review Mode`, and `Guardrails` now require a subagent or disposable worktree to inherit the resolved `headSha`; the `REVIEW REPORT` template opens with `Review target: PR # @ ` so a mismatch is visible in the artifact. - **`.agents/skills/ziw-code-review/references/remote-worker-review.md`** — the remote-worker prompt template carries `PR` and `Head SHA` instead of a loose `repo and branch or PR URL`. - **`.agents/skills/ziw-code-review/agents/openai.yaml`** — default prompt requires an explicit target. - **`scripts/resolve-review-target.test.mjs`** (new) — regression coverage under `//#test:scripts`, which runs in `pnpm verify:ci` and therefore in blocking `ci`. The guard sits on the CLI entrypoint, not on a pure helper: four of the seven tests spawn `resolve-review-target.mjs` as a subprocess with cwd set to a throwaway git repo on branch `spl-118-flag-editing`, asserting the ambient HEAD and branch name never appear in the output. ## Mutation proof Mutation: replaced the fail-loud in `parseTargetArgs` with an ambient fallback, reintroducing the defect — ```js if (chosen.length === 0) return { kind: "pr", value: "", repo: ..., json: ... }; ``` Result: **2 of 7 tests red, 2 assertions turned** — the `stderr` fail-loud contract assertion in *"the CLI fails loud instead of falling back to the ambient worktree"*, and the `assert.throws` in *"parsing keeps the target explicit and never invents a default"*. Reverted; 7/7 green. ## verify:ci First run was red on `//#format:check` (my two new files were formatted with a stray `npx biome` rather than the pinned repo binary), which cascaded into `//#knip`, `//#test:scripts`, and `@splitch/repo-lint#test`. Fixed with `pnpm exec biome format --write` and re-ran once: ``` Tasks: 85 successful, 85 total Cached: 82 cached, 85 total ``` The 3 uncached tasks are `//#format:check`, `//#knip`, and `//#test:scripts` — exactly the root tasks whose turbo inputs include `scripts/**`. No package I modified came back cached. ## Note for the repo owner `skills-lock.json` records these skills as vendored from `zaks-io/skills`. This change diverges the local copy; a future `ziw-setup` sync could overwrite it. Left the lock untouched rather than guessing its hash derivation. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) --- Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need. Autofix is disabled.

author: jingbanz
body:
## Summary

- define Core-owned workload timeout policy and apply the same live-coaching and history-compaction budgets to OpenAI, Claude Code, and Codex
- enforce one absolute auxiliary-request deadline across runtime setup and inference, passing only the remaining budget into the model turn
- recover a timed-out Codex turn with `turn/interrupt` plus matching terminal confirmation so a healthy shared app-server can serve the next attempt
- invalidate the Codex app-server only when the turn cannot be identified or interrupt/terminal cleanup leaves stream state uncertain
- keep history compaction fail-soft: timeout, empty output, or another failure preserves the full history for a later compaction attempt
- cover provider parity, end-to-end deadline accounting, and shared-server reuse with regression tests; update the design documentation

## Why

Timeouts describe Jarvis workloads, not providers. A single deadline also prevents setup and inference from each receiving a fresh timeout window. For Codex, scoped turn cancellation preserves the healthy transport while still ensuring late events from a timed-out turn cannot leak into the next request.

Closes #121.

## Validation

- `swift build` — passed
- `./scripts/run-tests.sh --filter CLIBrainClientTests` — passed, 17 tests
- `./scripts/run-tests.sh --filter CLIBrainRuntimeTests` — passed, 20 tests
- `./scripts/run-tests.sh --filter OpenAIBrainClientTests` — passed, 26 tests
- `./scripts/run-tests.sh --filter ScreenCaptureRunnerTests` — passed, 7 tests
- `SWT_EXPERIMENTAL_MAXIMUM_PARALLELIZATION_WIDTH=1 ./scripts/run-tests.sh` — passed, 577 tests in 65 suites (one opt-in screen-capture test skipped as expected)

Bug de **perda silenciosa de histórico** (validação do Wagner).

## Bug
Numa aba privada **ad-hoc** (setting "sempre privado" desligada), restaurar janelas/abas do Histórico as trazia **em privado** → privado não persiste histórico → as abas restauradas paravam de salvar histórico sem o usuário perceber.

`restaurarAbas` (usado pelo **restaurar-do-histórico** E pelo **restaurar-sessão**) e `reabrirFechada` (Ctrl+Shift+T) herdavam o `modoPrivado` ad-hoc da aba de origem.

Ações originadas do histórico/sessão **sempre** abrem em contexto **normal** (`privada=false`) + `setModoPrivado(false)` pra alinhar as próximas navegações. `registrarHistorico`/`abrirUrlLivre` ganham `privadoOverride` pra thread'ar o contexto explícito (o setState de `modoPrivado` só valeria no próximo tick, daí o override).

- `restaurarSessao`: via `restaurarAbas` (coberto).
- `reabrirFechada`: força normal pela mesma razão.

author: jonahgabriel
body:
Fixes the omnimarket `dev` trunk red on **FSM Handler Drift Guard**, and the same latent defect in the nightly delegation regression.

Ticket: **OMN-13953** — Runner workspace-hygiene fix — stale `../omnibase_core` sibling-clone collision.

## Diagnosis

The guard was **not** failing on drift. It died at step 2 of 10, before any derivation ran:

```
fatal: destination path '../omnibase_core' already exists and is not an empty directory.
##[error]Process completed with exit code 128.
```

Root cause: the runner job-started hook resets only `_work/<repo>/<repo>` —

```
[runner-job-started] Resetting workspace: /home/runner/actions-runner/_work/omnimarket/omnimarket
```

— never its **parent**. A step that clones a sibling repo into `../<name>` therefore leaves that directory behind for the next job on the same self-hosted runner, and the next `git clone` is non-idempotent.

**Why `push` failed while `pull_request` stayed green.** The `OMNI_RUNNER_SELECTOR_V1` block routes trusted events to the persistent self-hosted fleet and `pull_request` to ephemeral `ubuntu-latest`:

```yaml
runs-on: >-
  ${{ github.event_name != 'pull_request'
      && fromJSON(vars.OMNI_TRUSTED_CI_RUNS_ON_JSON || '["self-hosted","omnibase-ci"]')
      || fromJSON(vars.OMNI_PUBLIC_PR_RUNS_ON_JSON || '["ubuntu-latest"]') }}
```

So the red was only ever visible on the post-merge trunk signal, never on a PR.

### Two corrections to the reported framing

1. **#1985's core repin (`5a907b71` → `4d7c5fba`) did not cause this.** The guard never reached the code that consumes the pin. First red `push` run was **2026-07-29T02:42:22Z** (run `30417551946`, head `75b0e256`); last green `push` was **2026-07-29T01:49:44Z** (run `30415167141`, head `c0b5e325`). That is **39 consecutive `push` failures** predating #1985 by a full day. #1985 merely re-triggered a long-standing red.
2. **Future PRs do not inherit this red.** `fsm-handler-drift` is not a required status check on `omnimarket` `dev` or `main`, and PR-event runs execute on `ubuntu-latest` and pass. The blast radius is the post-merge trunk signal and the nightly — not PR mergeability.

## Fix

`plugin-compat-gate.yml` already carried the correct fix (a `Clean stale dependency clones` step, added in `de84a5f3`) and stayed green throughout. This PR applies that same precedent to the two workflows that lacked it, and generalizes it into an invariant. No allowlist, no derivation change — the guard's drift logic is untouched and was never implicated.

| Workflow | Live symptom before this PR |
|---|---|
| `validator-fsm-handler-drift.yml` | 39 consecutive `push` failures (2026-07-29T02:42Z to 2026-07-31T02:22Z) |
| `delegation-regression-nightly.yml` | 8 consecutive `schedule` failures (run `30526140685` and predecessors) |

Also adds `tests/ci/test_self_hosted_sibling_clone_hygiene.py`: on any job that can land on a persistent self-hosted runner, every `git clone ... ../<dir>` must be preceded **in execution order** by an `rm -rf` of that dir. This turns a one-off fix into a checked invariant so the class cannot silently recur (CLAUDE.md rule 5). It is a self-contained test in the existing `tests/ci/` suite — no new `scripts/` surface.

## dod_evidence

**RED-before / GREEN-after**, detector run against the real pre-fix blobs at `edc159955` and the post-fix tree:

```
=== detector vs PRE-fix blobs at edc159955 ===
  [RED  ] validator-fsm-handler-drift.yml: [('fsm-handler-drift', 'omnibase_core'), ('fsm-handler-drift', 'omnibase_compat')]
  [RED  ] delegation-regression-nightly.yml: [('golden-tasks', 'omnibase_core'), ('golden-tasks', 'omnibase_compat'), ('golden-tasks', 'omnimemory')]
  [green] plugin-compat-gate.yml: []

=== detector vs POST-fix working tree ===
  [green] validator-fsm-handler-drift.yml: []
```

author: juanjoselamarca
body:
Una cancha de 9 hoyos jugada a 18 se recorre **dos veces**. Es lo normal en Chile y el motor no lo sabía: pedía 18 hoyos a un catálogo de 9, no encontraba los hoyos 10-18 y los completaba a par 4 con stroke index inventado. Todo en silencio.

- El par de la ronda salía `36 + 9×4 = 72` en vez de `35 + 35 = 70`.
- Ese 72 entraba a la fórmula WHS contra un Course Rating de 9 hoyos, así que `(CR − par)` quedaba ~36 golpes corrido.
- Media vuelta se puntuaba contra par 4: birdies y bogeys mal contados, y golpes de handicap repartidos en el hoyo equivocado.

## Qué hace

**1. Modela la segunda vuelta de verdad.** `src/golf/courses/vueltas.ts` es la fuente única de tres conceptos que estaban re-derivados inline en cinco lugares: en qué escala está el dato, cuántas vueltas da la ronda, y qué hoyos se juegan. Los hoyos 10-18 son los 1-9 otra vez, con su par real y el stroke index de la tarjeta de 18 que imprime un club de 9 (impares la primera vuelta, pares la segunda — permutación exacta de 1..18). Course Rating y par son aditivos por vuelta; el slope no se escala.

**2. Guardarrail de rating incoherente (A1-A5).** Un rating que no cierra en ninguna escala ya no produce handicaps absurdos: el motor anula el término `(CR − par)` y el jugador recibe su índice. Y el organizador se entera **antes** de crear el torneo, no en el hoyo 7.

## La parte que no estaba planeada: reconciliar con el #293

El #293 aterrizó en `main` 18 horas después del último commit de esta rama y **cambió la premisa**: ahora el rating se *corrige* antes de usarlo (prueba las dos hipótesis de escala y, si ninguna cierra, devuelve el par). Auditando el número ya corregido, el guardarrail quedaba ciego justo donde importa: C.G. Río Blanco (55 contra par 35) salía con delta 0 y parecía sano.

Y al revés: el gate seguía bloqueando los 9 loops de Brisas, Marbella y Rocas (72 contra par 36) como si el motor no supiera qué hacer con ellos. Desde el #293 sí sabe.

`resolverRatingEnEscalaDe9` ahora devuelve **por qué** dio ese número — `ya_en_9`, `era_de_18` (RECUPERADO) o `imposible` — y cada consumidor mira lo que le corresponde: el motor usa el valor, el guardarrail mira la clasificación y juzga el dato **crudo** cuando es imposible.

### Impacto sobre el catálogo real (193 canchas, medido el 6-ago)

| | Antes | Después |
|---|---|---|
| Canchas bloqueadas (9h y 18h) | 11 | **2** — Río Blanco DAMAS y VARONES |
| Recorridos bloqueados | 3 clubes de 27 | **0** |
| Advertencias | 1 (Rinconada) | 1 (Rinconada) |

Brisas, Marbella y Rocas de Santo Domingo vuelven a servir para torneo neto. Bloquearlos era un falso positivo.

## "Un concepto, una fuente" ×5

| Concepto | Antes | Ahora |
|---|---|---|
| Par de la ronda de torneo | `courses.par_total ?? 72` en `/torneo` y el Resumen; `sumParDedupByHole(...)` en `/en-vivo` y `/tv` — **y las dos en `/en-vivo`**. 35 golpes de diferencia en una cancha de 9 jugada a 18 | `parDeLaRondaDelTorneo` |
| Umbral rating↔par | `BANDA_RATING_VS_PAR = 6` y `TOLERANCIA_RATING_9H = 5`, en archivos distintos | uno solo |
| Par cuando hay dos candidatos | regla inline del #293, y `parTotal ?? 72` a ciegas en las ramas de 18h | `parEnLaMismaEscala` |
| Hoyos de la tarjeta | idiom copiado en `/tarjeta/[id]` y `/perfil/historial/[id]`, con resultados distintos | `hoyosDeLaTarjeta` |
| De qué hoyo del catálogo sale cada hoyo | `vueltasDeLaRonda` re-derivado en los dos scorers, sin la guarda de catálogo sucio | campo `origen` |

## Code review

`superpowers:code-reviewer` devolvió **FAIL**: 2 bloqueantes, 2 importantes, 4 menores. Todos cerrados, con tests verificados por mutación.

El bloqueante real era una regresión introducida en este mismo PR: la columna HCP del board se degradaba al índice crudo en torneos de 9 hoyos, porque el lookup del CourseData de 18h recibía el par de la **ronda** (36) en vez del de la **cancha** (72). Se arregló en el motor, no en el caller.

Los hallazgos se verificaron contra el catálogo real: bajar la banda de escala de 6 a 5 no reclasifica ninguna de las 619 filas, y ningún loop hijo es de 18 hoyos.

## Verificación

- `tsc --noEmit` → 0 errores
- 3648 tests unitarios verdes
- 57 tests de integración **contra prod** verdes (catálogo, escala de rating, gate scorer↔board)
- `next build` OK · `next lint` 0 errores
- Impacto sobre el catálogo real medido dos veces (antes y después de los fixes del review), idéntico

## Lo que queda abierto

**Frente B (datos, no código):** cargar el `front_course_rating` / `front_slope_rating` real de los tees de Río Blanco (×2). No necesita la migración A5 — la validación de esas columnas ya acepta el rango de 9 hoyos.

**Deuda anotada:** `hoyosDeLaVuelta` reparte el stroke index de las dos vueltas asumiendo la convención chilena (impares la primera, pares la segunda). Es la que imprimen los clubes de 9 del catálogo, pero no es universal. Detalle en `docs/REORDENAMIENTO_TRACKING.md`.

author: shuvamk
body:
## Summary

This is items 1, 2 and 3 from your own review on #322, plus the CRLF nit from the same
comment. #322 was merged as a single commit (`31cd4ab0`) with no follow-up, so all four
still reproduce on `main` at `460b2547`. `apps/api/src/lib/ssh-tunnel.ts` had no test file
at all; this adds one.

Three things stated up front so you can weigh them before reading the diff:

- **The `Transfer-Encoding` casing bug is not observed against our own edge.** OpenResty
  emits lowercase `chunked`. This is robustness on a general-purpose HTTP/1.1 parser, not
  a fix for a reported outage.
- **The CRLF item has no reachable exploit today, and you said so yourself** in the #322
  review: *"no CRLF validation now that http.request isn't doing it (not reachable today —
  all callers encodeURIComponent)"*. I re-walked every mgmt path builder at this tip to
  confirm it still holds: each one is a string literal, or `encodeURIComponent(domain)`
  plus a derived number (`from`/`to` minutes, a `YYYYMMDD` string, `limit` clamped to
  1..200). The only `headers` object ever passed is the literal
  `{"Content-Type": "application/json"}`, and `method` is only ever `"GET"` or `"POST"`. It
  is here because `http.request` *was* enforcing this for free and the rewrite dropped it.
- **`main` CI is green** (run [30596928634](https://github.com/oblien/openship/actions/runs/30596928634),
  success at `460b2547`), so unlike my last few PRs there is no inherited red here — a red
  check on this one would be mine.

## Motivation

All four executed against the real parser with a stubbed `Duplex` in place of the SSH
channel.

| # | Input on the wire | Before | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` + `7\r\n{"a":1}\r\n0\r\n\r\n` | `body '{"a":1}'` | same (control) |
| 1 | `Transfer-Encoding: Chunked` + same body | `200, body '7\r\n{"a":1}\r\n0\r\n\r\n'` | `body '{"a":1}'` |
| 1 | `Transfer-Encoding: gzip, chunked` + same body | `200, body '7\r\n{"a":1}\r\n0\r\n\r\n'` | chunk framing stripped |
| 2 | `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` + `7\r\n{"a":1}\r\n`, socket closes (no `0` chunk) | `200, body '7\r\n{"a":1}\r\n'` | `null` |
| 2 | `Content-Length: 20` + 7 bytes, socket closes | `200, body '{"a":1}'` | `null` |
| 3 | SSE frame `data: {"city":"München"}\n\n` cut inside the two bytes of `ü` | relayed as `data: {"city":"M<ef bf bd><ef bf bd>nchen"}\n\n`, `Buffer.equals` false | byte-identical |
| 4 | path `/health\r\nX-Injected: yes\r\n\r\nGET /rules HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: 127.0.0.1:9145` | two complete HTTP requests written onto one socket | refused |
| 4 | header `{"X-Trace": "abc\r\nX-Injected: yes"}` | `...Connection: close\r\nX-Trace: abc\r\nX-Injected: yes\r\n\r\n` | refused |

Why each one matters:

1 and 2 both land the caller back in the exact silent-no-data symptom #322 was opened to
fix: `fetchMgmt` calls `JSON.parse(res.body)`, which throws on chunk framing or on a
truncated object, and the `catch` returns `null`. Case 2 is the realistic one — the SSH
channel dropping mid-scrape now yields a 200 with a partial body instead of an error, and
`mgmtRequest` never falls through to the exec transport because it got a truthy result.

3 is a transport-level correctness fix, and I want to be precise about what it does and
does not buy. `apps/api/test/lib/server-log-stream-framing.test.ts` already pins byte-exact
SSE relay for the **exec** transport ("Decoding each chunk as a string first would replace
the halves with U+FFFD"). The **tunnel** transport violated the same invariant, and after
this PR it doesn't: the bytes `tunnelStream` hands its caller are the bytes the edge sent.

**It does not fix the end-to-end live log tail on its own, and I don't want to imply it
does.** `serverLogStream` (`modules/projects/project.controller.ts:1236-1237`) is the sole
consumer of `mgmtStream`, and it does:

```ts
conn.stream.on("data", (chunk: Buffer) => {
  sseStream.write(chunk.toString()).catch(() => conn.destroy());
});
```

That `chunk.toString()` re-decodes every chunk and re-introduces exactly the same
corruption, on every mid-character chunk boundary for the life of the stream, and on the
**exec** transport too — so it is a strict superset of the site fixed here. I verified this
end to end through the patched transport into a real Hono `StreamingApi` (`write(string)`
runs the input back through `TextEncoder`); the browser still receives
`data: {"city":"M<ef bf bd><ef bf bd>nchen"}`.

One correction to something I'd assumed: the symptom is **silent corruption, not a dropped
frame**. U+FFFD is a legal character inside a JSON string, so the browser's `JSON.parse`
succeeds and returns `{"city":"M��nchen"}` — the log line renders with
replacement characters rather than failing loudly. So today, any hostname, path or
user-agent in a live tail containing a non-ASCII byte can render mangled, and nothing
reports an error.

4 is defence in depth only, per the disclaimer above.

One scoping note on the `gzip, chunked` row: this fixes the *framing* layer only. Nothing
here gunzips, so a genuinely gzipped body would still come back as gzip bytes rather than
JSON. That is not a regression — today it comes back as chunk framing wrapped around gzip
bytes — and adding content-coding support is a separate question I did not want to answer
unasked.

## Related issue

None — these are review comments on a merged PR.

## Changes

`apps/api/src/lib/ssh-tunnel.ts`, four commits, one per item:

- `isChunkedEncoding()` — lowercase, split on `,`, match any coding equal to `chunked`.
  Transfer-coding names are case-insensitive tokens and the header is a list
  (RFC 9110 §10.1.4). This is the shape you suggested.
- `contentLength`/`isChunked` hoisted out of the `data` handler (they derive from the head
  and never change), so `close` can tell the framings apart. Your gate verbatim: only a
  response with *no* length framing is terminated by the close itself; anything with a
  declared framing that hasn't already resolved is incomplete and returns `null`.
- `tunnelStream` accumulates a `Buffer` and slices bytes instead of `buffer += chunk.toString()`,
  mirroring the `Buffer.concat` head parser `tunnelRequest` already uses. Only the head is
  decoded to a string, which is ASCII by definition.
- `hasCrlf()` — both entry points return `null` before opening the SSH channel if the
  method, path, or any header name or value contains CR or LF. `null` is the failure mode
  both functions already document for a request they cannot make, and it lets `mgmtRequest`
  fall through to the exec transport, which `sq()`-quotes the URL.

**On the request head, nothing currently accepted changes behaviour** — two tests pin that
direction explicitly: a percent-encoded path plus a `Content-Type` header still goes out
byte-identical, and so does a normal `tunnelStream` head.

On the **response** side item 2 narrows what resolves, by design — that is the whole point
of it. One narrowing beyond the two truncation cases is worth calling out because it isn't
obvious from the diff: a malformed non-numeric `Content-Length` (e.g. `Content-Length: abc`)
makes `parseInt` return `NaN`, and `NaN !== null` holds, so `close` now takes the `else`
branch. Executed, same input either side:

| `Content-Length: abc` + `{"a":1}`, socket closes | `main` | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| | `{statusCode: 200, headers: {…}, body: '{"a":1}'}` | `null` |

I think `null` is right — a response whose framing header is unparseable is a response we
can't trust the length of, and `null` sends `mgmtRequest` to the exec transport rather than
handing `JSON.parse` a body of unknown completeness. But it is a behaviour change beyond
the two cases in the table above, it has no test of its own, and if you'd rather treat an
unparseable `Content-Length` as "no framing" (i.e. fall back to the close-terminated path)
that is a one-line change to `contentLength`'s initialiser: `Number.isNaN` → `null`.

**Deliberately not included**, to keep this to one concern:
